SafeProxy.masterCopy() short-circuit (SafeProxy.sol:53-68): selector check uses shr(224, calldataload(0)) so only the first 4 bytes matter; calldata shorter than 4 bytes cannot match (zero-padded); `shl(96, sload(0))` drops any dirty upper bits and mstore at 0x6c with return(0x60,0x20) yields 12 zero bytes (the untouched Solidity zero-slot, nothing runs before the assembly in the fallback) + 20-byte address = correct ABI encoding; tests 'should correctly mask the address value' and 'should ignore extra calldata bytes' cover this. Consequence that the singleton can never expose selector 0xa619486e is a known design choice. 2. SafeProxy delegatecall path (SafeProxy.sol:70-76): calldatacopy/returndatacopy/revert-bubbling correct; delegatecall ignores upper 96 bits of slot 0 (tested). A singleton without code would make the proxy silently succeed, but SafeProxyFactory.deployProxy (SafeProxyFactory.sol:55) checks extcodesize, SafeMigration constructor (SafeMigration.sol:59-61) and SafeToL2Setup.onlyContract (SafeToL2Setup.sol:54-57) also check code; constructor address(0) check at SafeProxy.sol:34 is present and tested. 3. SafeProxyFactory salt/front-running: salt = keccak(keccak(initializer), saltNonce[, chainid]) and the singleton is part of the CREATE2 init code (SafeProxyFactory.sol:57,88,119), so the owner set is bound to the address; a front-runner replaying identical calldata only deploys the victim's intended Safe (victim tx reverts 'Create2 call failed', tested). Cross-chain 'squatting' with different owners is impossible because the initializer hash is in the salt; createChainSpecificProxyWithNonce correctly includes chainid(). Factory and singletons are deployed via the chain-keyed safe-singleton-factory, so a same-address different-code singleton on another chain is not achievable by an attacker. 4. Initializer revert swallowing: `call` failure reverts the whole tx with bubbled data (SafeProxyFactory.sol:70-74), which also reverts the CREATE2, so a failed init never leaves an uninitialized proxy; only an empty or non-`setup` initializer leaves one claimable, which is documented in ISafe.sol:57 and tested ('should emit event without initializing'). 5. createProxyWithCallback: does not exist in 1.5.0 (removed in 1.4.0, CHANGELOG.md:146-150). 6. Safe.setup ordering/re-entrancy (Safe.sol:118-133): setupOwners sets threshold before internalSetFallbackHandler and setupModules, so re-entering setup from the `to` delegatecall or from the payment call reverts GS200; setupModules's GS100 check plus `isContract(to)`/GS000 are correct; the delegatecall is owner/deployer-trusted by design. handlePayment runs last; receiver re-entrancy cannot reach any privileged path. 7. Setup payment semantics (Safe.sol:129-133, 241-259): with native token the amount is `payment * min(1, tx.gasprice)`, so when tx.gasprice == 0 the relayer gets 0 (comment at Safe.sol:130-131 claims amount == payment). Only the relayer's own gas price is involved, so self-inflicted; informational, not reported. With paymentReceiver == 0 the payment goes to tx.origin, so a mempool front-runner of a factory deployment collects the relayer fee; the user's Safe is still created as intended — known relayer-side design (documented 'or 0 for tx.origin'), informational. 8. Self-owner privilege escalation on 1.5.0 (incl. 7702 self-ownership): `v==1` approval for owner == address(this) needs executor (msg.sender) == Safe or approvedHashes[Safe][hash], both of which already require an authorised Safe tx/module; the nested EIP-1271 path is closed because CompatibilityFallbackHandler.isValidSignature passes executor address(0) (CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:81-83) and SignatureVerifierMuxer does the same (line 159). No escalation. 9. isThisDelegatedAccount (EIP7702.sol:24-25): extcodecopy(address(),0,0,3) correctly reads the 0xef0100 designator (EXTCODECOPY returns the designator under EIP-7702, CODECOPY would not); memory-safe (scratch space); proxies/contracts can never start with 0xef0100 (EOF would be 0xef00). A 7702 EOA delegating to a proxy that delegatecalls the singleton still reports true, which is the intended semantics. 10. Storage layout: Safe linearization (Singleton -> ModuleManager.modules -> OwnerManager.owners/ownerCount/threshold -> Safe.nonce/_deprecatedDomainSeparator/signedMessages/approvedHashes) yields slots 0..8 exactly as SafeStorage.sol:14-54 and test/utils/storage.ts:11-46; all mixins (SelfAuthorized, ErrorMessage, Executor, EIP7702, EIP7951, SignatureDecoder, SecuredTokenTransfer, SecuredSignatureValidator, FallbackManager, StorageAccessible, NativeCurrencyPaymentFallback) declare no state variables; test/core/Safe.Storage.spec.ts and SafeToL2Setup.spec.ts 'follows the expected storage layout' assert it. The layout is identical to 1.0.0-1.4.1 (slot 6 = domainSeparator in <=1.2.0, deprecated since 1.3.0); keccak slots for fallback handler/guard unchanged; module-guard slot is new and zero. Migration tests from 1.1.1/1.2.0/1.3.0/1.4.1 (L1 and L2) pass. 11. SafeMigration (SafeMigration.sol:45-48, 71-100): onlyDelegateCall via immutable MIGRATION_SINGLETON is correct; callable only through the Safe's own delegatecall (execTransaction with threshold signatures or a trusted module); `ISafe(this).setFallbackHandler` is an external self-call that passes `authorized` and runs on the new singleton (layout-compatible). No version check, but all supported versions share the layout; a 7702 EOA delegating to SafeMigration itself would only write its own slot 0. Tests assert owner/threshold/nonce/guard slots untouched. 12. SafeToL2Setup (SafeToL2Setup.sol:64-69): onlyDelegateCall + onlyNonceZero + onlyContract; since execTransaction increments nonce before execute, it is unusable after the first Safe tx (tested 'can only be used through Safe initialization process'); during setup the caller already controls the `to` delegatecall so choosing an arbitrary l2Singleton grants no extra power and the choice is committed in the CREATE2 address; chainid()==1 no-op path tested. `ProxyCreation` event still reports the L1 singleton while ChangedMasterCopy is emitted from the proxy — intended, informational. A user could brick their own Safe by passing l2Singleton == proxy or == the lib (self-chosen). 13. Migrate_1_3_0_to_1_2_0 example: delegatecall-only check via immutable; writes the 1.2.0 chainId-less domain separator (typehash matches test expectation). Downgrading silently stops enforcing transaction/module guards and re-enables cross-chain signature replay, but it is an un-deployed example requiring owner authorisation — informational. 14. 7702 EOA as `_singleton`/`to`/`l2Singleton`/`gasToken` (passes extcodesize checks, code mutable by the EOA): all deployer/owner-chosen inputs, no third-party attack path. 15. Singleton self-use: constructor threshold=1 blocks setup on the singleton; it has no owners, modules[SENTINEL]==0, so execTransaction/execTransactionFromModule/authorized functions are unreachable on it. 16. 7702 storage persistence across re-delegation (another wallet implementation could zero slot 4 and make setup callable again when re-delegating to Safe) is user-controlled and inherent to EIP-7702, not a Safe defect. 17. 0.8.x build: SafeProxy/Factory/Migration/SafeToL2Setup/example contain no arithmetic that behaves differently; `abi.encode(..., this)` is valid in both.

findings.title: ExtensibleFallbackHandler: any address can self-register as a "Safe"; third-party IFallbackMethod/ISafeSignatureVerifier contracts must not treat msg.sender == ExtensibleFallbackHandler (or the `sender` argument) as proof of a legitimate Safe context
findings.description: `onlySelf` (ExtensibleBase.sol:39) only requires `_msgSender() == _manager()`, i.e. that the last 20 bytes of calldata equal `msg.sender`. When the handler is called directly (not through a Safe's FallbackManager), any EOA/contract can append its own address and pass the check, so `setSafeMethod` (FallbackHandler.sol:24-26), `setDomainVerifier` (SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:79-84) and `setSupportedInterface`/`add|removeSupportedInterfaceBatch` (ERC165Handler.sol:34-85) succeed with the caller's own address as the storage key. The caller can then invoke `FallbackHandler.fallback` (FallbackHandler.sol:31-41) directly with an arbitrary trailing 20 bytes, and the registered custom handler receives `handle(safe = attacker, sender = <attacker-chosen>, 0, data)` with `msg.sender == ExtensibleFallbackHandler`. Likewise `SignatureVerifierMuxer.isValidSignature` (SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:93-139) will call `verifier.isValidSafeSignature(safe = attacker, sender = <attacker-chosen>, ...)` for a verifier the attacker registered under their own key. The Safe itself is not affected (all state is keyed by `msg.sender`, and a Safe's entries can only be written when the Safe is `msg.sender` and the appended caller is the Safe, which only Safe transactions/modules can produce), but the ISafeSignatureVerifier docs (SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:17-29) and IFallbackMethod interface (ExtensibleBase.sol:8-14) do not warn that `safe` may be an arbitrary non-Safe address and that `sender` is attacker-controlled in that case.
findings.attack_path: 1) Attacker A sends tx to ExtensibleFallbackHandler with data = setSafeMethod(sel, encode(false, H)) || A (20 bytes). onlySelf passes because last-20-bytes == msg.sender == A; safeMethods[A][sel] = H. 2) A sends tx to ExtensibleFallbackHandler with data = sel || X (any 20 bytes). fallback() calls H.handle(safe=A, sender=X, 0, sel) with msg.sender == ExtensibleFallbackHandler. 3) If H (a third-party handler shared by many Safes) has any logic that trusts `msg.sender == EFH` as proof that `safe` is a configured Safe, or trusts `sender` globally (e.g. 'privileged address X interacted'), it is misled. Victim Safes' own safeMethods/domainVerifiers entries are untouched (verified).
findings.evidence: PoC run in this session (hardhat, 0.7.6): after a direct call `setSafeMethod(0xdeadbeef, encode(false, Recorder)) || attacker`, `efh.safeMethods(attacker, sel) == encoded` while `efh.safeMethods(victimSafe, sel) == 0x0`; calling victimSafe with `0xdeadbeef` reverts 'method handler not set'; a direct call `0xdeadbeef || 0x1111…1111` made Recorder observe `lastMsgSender == EFH`, `lastSafe == attacker`, `lastSender == 0x1111…1111`. Same for `setDomainVerifier`: `domainVerifiers(attacker, d) == Recorder`, `domainVerifiers(victimSafe, d) == 0`. Code: ExtensibleBase.sol:35-41 (onlySelf), HandlerContext.sol:47-56 (_msgSender reads last 20 bytes), HandlerContext.sol:62-64 (_manager = msg.sender), FallbackHandler.sol:31-41.
findings.recommendation: Document in IFallbackMethod/IStaticFallbackMethod and ISafeSignatureVerifier natspec that `safe` is simply the `msg.sender` of the ExtensibleFallbackHandler and may be any address (not necessarily a Safe), and that `sender` is only trustworthy when `safe` is a >=1.3.0 Safe. Third-party handlers/verifiers should key all state by `safe` and never use `msg.sender == ExtensibleFallbackHandler` as an authorization signal on its own. Optionally, `onlySelf` could additionally require `_requireFallback()`-style evidence (msg.sender.getStorageAt(FALLBACK_HANDLER_STORAGE_SLOT) == address(this)), which would reject direct self-registration by non-Safes, though that is a behavior change.

findings.title: HandlerContext/ExtensibleFallbackHandler `onlySelf` is fully spoofable if the handler is installed on a pre-1.3.0 Safe (FallbackManager that does not append the caller), enabling arbitrary domain-verifier installation and ERC-1271 signature forgery for that Safe
findings.description: `_msgSender()` (HandlerContext.sol:47-56) returns the last 20 bytes of calldata and is only meaningful when `msg.sender` is a FallbackManager that appends `caller()` (FallbackManager.sol:70-78, introduced in 1.3.0). Safe 1.1.1/1.2.0 `FallbackManager` forwards calldata verbatim. `onlySelf` (ExtensibleBase.sol:39) compares `_msgSender()` with `msg.sender`; behind a legacy Safe, any external caller can satisfy it by appending the Safe's own address. This is acknowledged in natspec (HandlerContext.sol:41-44 'only reliable with a FallbackManager supporting this (e.g. Safe contract >=1.3.0)'; ExtensibleFallbackHandler.sol:143 'Designed to be used with Safe >= 1.3.0') but the concrete consequence, full ERC-1271 forgery via `setDomainVerifier`, is not spelled out, and nothing in the handler prevents a legacy Safe from calling `setFallbackHandler(EFH)` (1.1.1 already has setFallbackHandler). Not reproducible in this repo (no pre-1.3.0 artifacts), so reported as informational.
findings.attack_path: Precondition: a Safe < 1.3.0 (fallback forwards calldata without appending caller) has set ExtensibleFallbackHandler as its fallback handler. 1) Attacker calls legacySafe with data = setDomainVerifier(D, EvilVerifier) || legacySafe (20 bytes). legacySafe forwards unchanged to EFH; msg.sender == legacySafe, _msgSender() == legacySafe → onlySelf passes; domainVerifiers[legacySafe][D] = EvilVerifier (SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:79-84). 2) For any EIP-712 domain D used by a protocol the Safe interacts with (e.g. Permit2, Seaport, CoW), attacker builds a signature `0x5fd7e97d || D || typeHash || encodeData || payload` whose _hash matches; isValidSignature (SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:107-132) routes to EvilVerifier which returns the magic value → protocol accepts a forged Safe signature and moves the Safe's approved assets. Same spoof lets the attacker install non-static custom methods via setSafeMethod.
findings.evidence: HandlerContext.sol:47-56 (_msgSender reads calldata tail with no trusted-forwarder check), ExtensibleBase.sol:35-41 (onlySelf), SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:79-84 and 107-132 (verifier selection by attacker-supplied domainSeparator from the authorized mapping), FallbackManager.sol:70-78 (1.5.0 appends caller; legacy versions did not). Natspec acknowledgements at HandlerContext.sol:41-44 and ExtensibleFallbackHandler.sol:143.
findings.recommendation: Make the >=1.3.0 requirement enforceable rather than advisory, e.g. have `onlySelf` additionally call `_requireFallback()` (HandlerContext.sol:33-37), which on a legacy Safe without getStorageAt reverts and on a 1.3.0+ Safe passes; or at minimum expand the ExtensibleFallbackHandler/HandlerContext natspec to state that installing it on a Safe whose FallbackManager does not append the caller allows anyone to configure methods and verifiers and therefore forge ERC-1271 signatures.

findings.title: Per-Safe ExtensibleFallbackHandler configuration (safeMethods, domainVerifiers, safeInterfaces) lives in the shared handler's storage, survives fallback-handler and owner changes, and is not enumerable on-chain
findings.description: `domainVerifiers` (SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:64), `safeMethods` (ExtensibleBase.sol:32) and `safeInterfaces` (ERC165Handler.sol:25) are keyed by Safe address in the singleton handler. Switching the Safe's fallback handler away from EFH (FallbackManager.sol:46-49) does not clear them, and switching back re-activates them instantly. Unlike modules (`getModulesPaginated`) or the guard/handler slots (`getStorageAt`), there is no on-chain enumeration; discovery requires scanning `ChangedDomainVerifier`/`ChangedSafeMethod` events. A domain verifier is an ERC-1271 signing oracle for one EIP-712 domain, so a stale entry is a signature backdoor.
findings.attack_path: 1) While in control, a (later-rotated) owner set executes setDomainVerifier(D_permit2, EvilVerifier) through the Safe. 2) Ownership is transferred (swapOwner/addOwner/removeOwner); new owners audit owners, threshold, modules, guard and fallback handler (canonical EFH) and see nothing wrong. 3) Old owner later presents `0x5fd7e97d || D_permit2 || …` signatures to Permit2; SignatureVerifierMuxer.isValidSignature routes to EvilVerifier (SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:123-131) and the Safe's ERC-20 allowances are drained. Same if the Safe temporarily moved to CompatibilityFallbackHandler and later back to EFH: the old verifier/methods are live again with no event at re-enable time.
findings.evidence: SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:64, 79-84 (mapping keyed by Safe; only setter is setDomainVerifier, never cleared on handler change); ExtensibleBase.sol:32, 45-60; ERC165Handler.sol:25; FallbackManager.sol:19-49 (setFallbackHandler only writes the slot). No enumeration function exists in any in-scope file (only public mapping getters).
findings.recommendation: Document that operators must audit `ChangedDomainVerifier`/`ChangedSafeMethod` events (or the mapping getters for known domains) on ownership transfer or when re-enabling the EFH. Consider adding an on-chain enumerable structure or a `clearConfiguration()`-style `onlySelf` helper so a Safe can atomically wipe all handler state, and/or emitting a configuration-version event.

result.reviewed: Read end to end: contracts/handler/CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol, contracts/handler/HandlerContext.sol, contracts/handler/TokenCallbackHandler.sol, contracts/handler/ExtensibleFallbackHandler.sol, contracts/handler/extensible/{ERC165Handler,ExtensibleBase,FallbackHandler,MarshalLib,SignatureVerifierMuxer,TokenCallbacks}.sol, contracts/base/FallbackManager.sol, contracts/interfaces/IFallbackManager.sol, contracts/common/StorageAccessible.sol (getStorageAt, simulateAndRevert), contracts/common/SecuredSignatureValidator.sol (#1115), contracts/common/SignatureDecoder.sol, contracts/libraries/SafeStorage.sol, contracts/libraries/SignMessageLib.sol, Safe.sol:255-470 (checkContractSignature, checkSignatures, checkNSignatures, legacy checkSignatures/checkNSignatures, approveHash, domainSeparator), ModuleManager.getModulesPaginated, OwnerManager.requireIsValidOwner (GS203), common/EIP7702.sol, NativeCurrencyPaymentFallback.receive. Tests: test/handlers/{CompatibilityFallbackHandler,HandlerContext,TokenCallbackHandler,ExtensibleFallbackHandler}.spec.ts, test/utils/{contracts.ts (KillLib, BadSimulator, RevertingValidator), extensible.ts, setup.ts}, contracts/test/{TestHandler,ERC1155Token,TestSafeSignatureVerifier}.sol. Docs: docs/signatures.md, docs/overview.md fallback section, git diff of #1123 (f8fc2f2). Ran: `npx hardhat test test/handlers/CompatibilityFallbackHandler.spec.ts test/handlers/HandlerContext.spec.ts` (31 passing, incl. the new 'should propagate exact revert data'), plus a temporary PoC spec (3 experiments, since removed) covering direct self-registration on the EFH, a simulate() payload that absorbs the appended caller, and 1-3-byte calldata completing a selector with the caller address prefix.
result.ruled_out: 1) _msgSender()/_manager() spoofing against a >=1.3.0 Safe: FallbackManager.fallback (FallbackManager.sol:70-78) always appends caller() after the full calldata, so the last 20 bytes are the true caller; a caller cannot place bytes after it. onlySelf therefore requires the original caller to BE the Safe, achievable only via execTransaction(to=self), modules, owner delegatecall, or (reverted) simulateAndRevert targets. Direct calls to the handler can only write entries keyed by msg.sender (PoC confirmed victim entries untouched). 2) onlyFallback/_requireFallback 'trick' (a non-Safe implementing getStorageAt to return the handler): documented best-effort (HandlerContext.sol:18-31) and explicitly tested ('can be tricked into sending tokens to the fallback handler'); consequence is only tokens locked in the handler. 3) CompatibilityFallbackHandler.isValidSignature executor semantics: passes address(0) (CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:83); address(0) can never be an owner (OwnerManager.sol:120 GS203; checkNSignatures rejects currentOwner <= lastOwner with lastOwner=0 and owners[0]==0, Safe.sol ~line 410). So v==1 entries need an explicit approveHash of the SafeMessage hash, which is intended. Legacy msg.sender-executor overloads (Safe.sol:422-442) are not used by handlers. 4) Message/transaction hash replay: SafeMessage hash = keccak(0x1901||domainSeparator(chainid,safe)||keccak(SAFE_MSG_TYPEHASH, keccak(abi.encode(_dataHash)))) (CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:51-54,76-77); SAFE_TX_TYPEHASH differs and struct-hash preimages differ in length; domain binds chain+Safe; both handlers and SignMessageLib use identical SAFE_MSG_TYPEHASH (verified constants). A signature on txHash cannot validate as a message and vice versa. 5) Self-referential contract signatures (Safe as its own owner is only possible for EIP-7702 delegated accounts, OwnerManager.sol:120): each nesting level wraps the hash in another SafeMessage layer and needs threshold real signers; recursion ends in OOG inside the staticcall → GS024. No self-approval. 6) simulate() (#1123): response := mload(0x40) == ptr; returndatacopy(response, 0x20, L+0x20) writes [L][data]; mload(response) == L exactly, so revert(add(response,0x20), mload(response)) returns precisely the inner revert data (previously 32 extra bytes). Success flag at scratch 0x00 is never overwritten (response >= 0x80). If a real Safe is caller(), L == inner returndatasize so copy is in bounds; if L is forged by a non-Safe caller (incl. the 2^256-0x20 overflow making responseEncodedSize 0 and mload(response) read the stale copied selector word), the only outcome is returndatacopy OOB revert or OOG in the caller's own frame; no state is touched, and BadSimulator test modes 0-3 cover the malformed cases. The outer Safe.simulateAndRevert always reverts so the delegatecalled target (running in the Safe's context, msg.sender = handler) cannot persist anything. 7) simulate() calldata forwarding with the appended caller: the handler copies calldata verbatim (incl. the 20 trailing bytes) to the Safe; the Safe's ABI decoder ignores trailing bytes. A crafted `calldataPayload` length can absorb the appended 20 bytes (PoC confirmed the inner msg.data was echoSelector||caller) but that only injects the caller's own address, which the caller could have supplied anyway. 8) 1-3-byte calldata through the Safe: 0-byte calls go to receive() (NativeCurrencyPaymentFallback.sol:15) so never reach a handler; for 1-3 bytes the appended caller address completes the 4-byte selector; only argument-less handler functions can be dispatched (0.7 ABI decoder reverts on short calldata), i.e. CompatibilityFallbackHandler.getModules() (PoC confirmed with a 0xf3-prefixed contract: returns the view result). No state-changing or auth-bearing function is reachable; the FallbackManager GS400 check (FallbackManager.sol:33) already addresses the self-handler variant. 9) #1115 SecuredSignatureValidator as reached via handler isValidSignature: staticcall + `success && result.length == 32 && abi.decode == bytes32(magic)` is strictly tighter than the previous high-level call (rejects extra return data, dirty bytes4 padding, no-code owners → GS024). Handler isValidSignature functions are view and return exactly 32 bytes; nested Safe-owner validation through FallbackManager.fallback uses CALL with value 0, which is permitted inside STATICCALL. 10) SignatureVerifierMuxer verifier selection: verifier is looked up under the Safe's own authorization for the signature-supplied domainSeparator and only used if keccak(0x1901||D||keccak(typeHash||encodeData)) == _hash (SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:121-131), so forging a verifier for a hash in another domain requires a keccak preimage; test 'should revert it trying to forge the domain separator' covers it. Accidental routing of a normal packed signature requires an ECDSA r starting with 0x5fd7e97d AND an authorized verifier at that random 32-byte key (negligible); length>=68 guard prevents abi.decode reverts for short sigs. Malformed offsets after the prefix revert instead of falling back, but only the caller is affected. 11) IStaticFallbackMethod.handle is declared view, so Solidity emits STATICCALL for isStatic handlers (FallbackHandler.sol:37); 'static' is enforced, not advisory. fallback(bytes calldata) returns `result` raw (not re-encoded), matching the Mirror test expectation. value is always 0 because FallbackManager.fallback is non-payable. 12) MarshalLib dirty bits: decode masks the address to 160 bits and derives isStatic solely from the top byte (MarshalLib.sol:40-41); bytes 1..11 are ignored; decodeWithSelector's shl(168, shr(160, data)) places the selector in the top 4 bytes (pad bytes land below and the `interfaceId == _interfaceId` check and Solidity cleanup make a mismatch fail closed). Only the Safe itself can supply these values. 13) ERC165Handler: 0xffffffff cannot be set (ERC165Handler.sol:37); setSupportedInterface uses _manager() while batch functions use _msgSender(), equal under onlySelf; empty batch sets interface 0x00000000 (harmless). 14) TokenCallbackHandler/TokenCallbacks returning selectors unconditionally: only effect is that Safes accept all ERC-721/1155 tokens; tokensReceived is unguarded but ERC-777 `send` to the handler reverts (no ERC-1820 implementer can be registered for the handler), `transfer` lock-up is the generic warning at TokenCallbackHandler.sol:13-15. 15) getModules(): returns first 10 modules only, as documented (CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:88-97); getModulesPaginated argument validation (GS105/GS106) is satisfied by SENTINEL/10. 16) No delegatecall or selfdestruct exists in any handler; the only delegatecall is inside Safe.simulateAndRevert and always reverts. 17) Memory safety of FallbackManager.fallback and simulate(): both use scratch beyond the free memory pointer only inside assembly and end the frame or update 0x40 before returning to Solidity; no Solidity allocation interleaves. 18) Reentrancy via non-static custom handlers or domain verifiers: callbacks run with msg.sender = handler/verifier, not the Safe, so they gain no Safe authority; with the 'trusted handler' threat model this is by design.

findings.title: MultiSend / MultiSendCallOnly: invalid operation byte reverts with stale returndata of the previous sub-call
findings.description: In both batch libraries the `switch operation` has only `case 0` / `case 1` (MultiSend.sol:62-68, MultiSendCallOnly.sol:53-60); for any other operation byte `success` stays 0 and the generic failure path runs: `returndatacopy(ptr, 0, returndatasize()); revert(ptr, returndatasize())` (MultiSend.sol:69-73, MultiSendCallOnly.sol:61-65). `returndatasize()` at that point is NOT empty: it is the return data of the previous *successful* sub-call in the same batch, because the EVM returndata buffer is only replaced by the next CALL/DELEGATECALL. The batch therefore reverts with an unrelated payload. Confirmed with a PoC (docs/security-review/poc/libraries-parsing-edgecases.spec.ts, test 'invalid operation reverts with the *previous* sub-call's return data'): entry 1 is a successful CALL whose return bytes are `abi.encodeWithSignature("Error(string)","NOT A REVERT")`, entry 2 has operation=2; the delegatecall reverts with `Error("NOT A REVERT")` although nothing reverted. Only the single-entry case (covered by the existing test 'Should fail when using invalid operation', which expects `revertedWithoutReason`) yields empty revert data. Atomicity is preserved (the batch always reverts), so there is no fund-safety impact; the issue is a misleading revert reason that can send tooling/simulators (which decode `Error(string)`/custom errors) and users down the wrong path, and it was not noticed because the existing test only covers the first-entry case.
findings.attack_path: No attacker path: the batch payload is owner-signed and the outcome is a revert either way. Robustness only: a batch with [successful call returning bytes X][entry with op >= 2] reverts with X, misattributing the failure.
findings.evidence: contracts/libraries/MultiSend.sol:61-73 (`let success := 0`, switch without default, failure path copies `returndatasize()` which still holds the previous sub-call's output); contracts/libraries/MultiSendCallOnly.sol:52-65 identical structure. PoC passes: 6 passing in docs/security-review/poc/libraries-parsing-edgecases.spec.ts.
findings.recommendation: Add a `default { revert(0, 0) }` branch to the `switch operation` (one line, no gas impact on the happy path) so an unsupported operation reverts with empty data, and extend test/libraries/MultiSend*.spec.ts with a two-entry case (successful call followed by op=2) asserting `revertedWithoutReason`.

findings.title: MultiSend packed parser has no bounds validation: loop bound is header-offset vs header-less length, over-long dataLength is zero-filled, short trailing bytes are silently ignored
findings.description: `let length := mload(transactions)` is the byte length of the payload, but the cursor `i` starts at 0x20 (MultiSend.sol:40) and the loop condition is `lt(i, length)` (MultiSend.sol:43; MultiSendCallOnly.sol:34), i.e. a header-inclusive offset is compared against a header-exclusive length. The bound is effectively off by 32 bytes; this is masked only because every entry is at least 85 bytes (MultiSend.sol:60,75), so a well-formed last entry always starts at `i <= length - 53 < length`. Consequences verified with the PoC in docs/security-review/poc/libraries-parsing-edgecases.spec.ts: (1) `dataLength` (MultiSend.sol:58) is never checked against the remaining bytes; a declared length that overshoots the array reads memory past the ABI-decoded `bytes` which, in the fresh DELEGATECALL frame, is all zero (the 0.7.6 calldata-to-memory decoder zero-terminates and nothing in the loop writes memory on the success path: all sub-calls use `out=0,outsize=0`). The target thus receives the real bytes followed by zero padding (test: 4 provided bytes, 68 declared, callee saw 68 bytes = 0xdeadbeef||64 zero bytes). No garbage can be executed. (2) 1..31 trailing bytes after the last well-formed entry are silently dropped because `i >= length` exits the loop. (3) 33..84 trailing bytes are parsed as a truncated entry whose missing fields read as zero (op 0, value 0, dataLength 0; `to` possibly partially present and, if zero, remapped to `address(this)` at MultiSend.sol:54 so the Safe calls its own `receive()`). (4) A `dataLength` large enough to wrap the cursor `i := add(i, add(0x55, dataLength))` (MultiSend.sol:75) cannot survive: the CALL/DELEGATECALL with that `argsSize` triggers unbounded memory expansion and runs out of gas before `i` is updated (PoC test passes with 5M gas). Everything here is deterministic over an owner-signed payload, so it is a strictness/robustness observation rather than a vulnerability; the behaviour has been identical since the original Gnosis MultiSend and both 1.5.0 audits had the file in scope (Certora scope list lines 189-190, Ackee 'all Solidity files in contracts').
findings.attack_path: None: the packed payload is part of the EIP-712 signed `data`, so an owner quorum would be the only party able to craft a malformed batch, and the effect is bounded (zero padding or dropped bytes). Off-chain decoders that are stricter than the contract could disagree with on-chain execution for malformed batches, which is a UX concern for signers at most.
findings.evidence: contracts/libraries/MultiSend.sol:39-43 (length vs i), :58 (dataLength unchecked), :75 (cursor advance); contracts/libraries/MultiSendCallOnly.sol:30-34, :49, :67. PoC: tests 'over-long dataLength reads zero-filled memory...', 'trailing bytes shorter than 32 are silently ignored...', 'huge dataLength cannot wrap the cursor...' all pass.
findings.recommendation: If stricter parsing is ever desired: compute `let end := add(0x20, length)`, loop while `lt(i, end)`, and `require(lte(add(i, add(0x55, dataLength)), end))` per entry (reverting on truncated entries and trailing bytes). Otherwise document the lenient behaviour in the NatSpec so decoders (SDK/UI/guards) mirror it exactly.

findings.title: MultiSend / MultiSendCallOnly remap `to == address(0)` to `address(this)`: a semantic divergence from <=1.4.1 that MultiSend-aware guards and decoders must account for
findings.description: Both batch libraries now execute `to := or(to, mul(iszero(to), address()))` (MultiSend.sol:54, MultiSendCallOnly.sol:45), so an entry with `to = 0x0` becomes a CALL to the Safe itself (msg.sender == Safe, which satisfies `SelfAuthorized.requireSelfCall` at contracts/common/SelfAuthorized.sol:16), e.g. `addOwnerWithThreshold`, `enableModule`, `setGuard`, `setFallbackHandler`. In 1.3.0/1.4.1 the same bytes meant a CALL to the zero address (an ETH burn / no-op). The code was present at both 1.5.0 audited commits (verified by fetching 1c8b24a0 and 5d265053: line 50 in each) and is tested ('forwards the call to self when to is zero address'), so it is accepted design. The reason it is worth recording: the encoding is otherwise byte-compatible with the 1.3.0/1.4.1 libraries (MultiSendCallOnly.sol:14-15 explicitly advertises compatibility), and nothing in CHANGELOG.md for 1.5.0 mentions the change (grep for the self-default returns only the 1.3.0 payable note at CHANGELOG.md:703). Third-party components that decode `multiSend` payloads with the old semantics, in particular transaction guards or Roles-style modifiers that implement a *deny* rule such as 'no batch entry may target the Safe itself' by comparing `to != address(safe)`, will treat a `to = 0x0` entry as harmless while on-chain it executes a privileged self-call.
findings.attack_path: Requires a quorum of owners (the batch is signed) plus an external guard/decoder that enforces restrictions on owners using the 1.4.1 interpretation of `to`. Owners sign a MultiSend batch containing `[op=0][to=0x00..00][value=0][len][addOwnerWithThreshold(attacker,1)]`; a guard that decodes the batch and denies entries with `to == safe` lets it through because it sees `to == 0x0`; MultiSend remaps it and the Safe adds the owner. No in-repo guard (contracts/examples/guards/*) decodes MultiSend, so there is no exploitable instance in this repository.
findings.evidence: contracts/libraries/MultiSend.sol:52-54 and contracts/libraries/MultiSendCallOnly.sol:43-45 (`to := or(to, mul(iszero(to), address()))`); test/libraries/MultiSend.spec.ts:316-348 and MultiSendCallOnly.spec.ts:241-273 show the intended self-call; upstream commits 1c8b24a0a438e8c2cd089a9d830d1688a47a28d5 and 5d26505388e9ee014ad9ac497aa48e3a13426eb1 both contain the line (audited).
findings.recommendation: Document the `to == 0 => address(this)` rule prominently in the 1.5.0 CHANGELOG/NatSpec and in integration guidance for guard/decoder authors (treat `to == 0` as `to == safe` when evaluating policies). The guards lens should check any MultiSend-aware policy code for this case.

Initcode revert reasons are swallowed into 'Could not deploy contract' (UX only, no security consequence, Certora I-03 already covered readability). 8) SignMessageLib has no onlyDelegateCall but is safe when called directly: `getMessageHash` calls `ISafe(address(this)).domainSeparator()` (SignMessageLib.sol:43) which the singleton does not implement and it has no fallback, so direct calls revert before any sstore (tests 'can only if msg.sender provides domain separator' / 'can be used only via DELEGATECALL opcode', and my PoC). Under delegatecall it writes `signedMessages[msgHash]` at slot keccak(h . 7) which matches Safe.sol:87 (slot 7) per the layout check above and the test 'changes the expected storage slot without touching the most important ones' (slot 7 asserted). Domain binding: identical construction to CompatibilityFallbackHandler.encodeMessageDataForSafe (handler lines 53-55) using the live `domainSeparator()` (chainid+address, Safe.sol:456-474), so `isValidSignature(hash, "")` with `signedMessages` lookup (handler :76-79) matches `signMessage(abi.encode(hash))`; chain-id is bound at signing time (expected). `singleton` being private in Singleton.sol vs internal in SafeStorage has no layout effect. 9) SimulateTxAccessor: immutable-based onlyDelegateCall (SimulateTxAccessor.sol:15-28) verified by test and PoC; `simulate` is reachable only through `simulateAndRevert`, whose unconditional revert discards all state changes; return-data assembly (:55-68) correctly bumps the free memory pointer by rds+0x20, stores length then data, so ABI encoding of (estimate, success, returnData) is well-formed; `estimate = startGas - gasleft()` cannot underflow; `Enum.Operation` is range-checked by the 0.7.6 ABI decoder; DelegateCall ignores `value` exactly as Safe.execute does (consistent). 10) StorageAccessible.simulateAndRevert (:35-48): delegatecall then `[success][returndatasize][returndata]` written at mload(0x40) and reverted with size rds+0x40; layout matches IStorageAccessible docs and the consumer in CompatibilityFallbackHandler.simulate (:143-176). findings.title: ReentrancyTransactionGuard lock can be cleared or set by anyone (no caller authorization), defeating the reentrancy protection
findings.description: The guard keeps one boolean in its own storage (GUARD_STORAGE_SLOT, ReentrancyTransactionGuard.sol:12, read via getGuard() at :29-37). checkTransaction (:43-60) does `require(!guard.active); guard.active = true;` and checkAfterExecution (:66-68) does `getGuard().active = false;` and checkModuleTransaction/checkAfterModuleExecution (:78-98) do the same on the same slot. None of the four functions checks msg.sender (e.g. that the caller is the Safe that configured the guard), so any address can flip the flag at will. Consequence A (bypass): while Safe tx T1 is executing (flag set at Safe.sol:175-190, before execute at :203), the callee of T1 calls guard.checkAfterExecution(0,false) directly, clearing the flag, then re-enters safe.execTransaction with the already-signed next-nonce tx T2 (nonce was pre-incremented at Safe.sol:168, so T2 is valid); checkTransaction now passes. The guard's sole stated purpose ("Prevents reentrancy into the transaction execution function", :8) does not hold against any callee. Consequence B (griefing DoS): any EOA can call checkTransaction(...) directly and set the flag; every Safe using that guard instance then reverts in execTransaction with "Reentrancy detected" until someone calls checkAfterExecution (also permissionless), so the lock is a per-block race the attacker can keep re-winning for the cost of gas. Both are reproduced by the PoC spec docs/security-review/poc/guards-reentrancy-debug.spec.ts (tests "a callee can clear the lock and re-enter execTransaction" and "anyone can lock the guard"), which pass against HEAD.
findings.attack_path: Bypass: 1) Safe S has ReentrancyTransactionGuard G set. 2) Owners have signed T1 (nonce n, to = untrusted contract A, or any call chain that reaches attacker code) and T2 (nonce n+1), e.g. both queued in the Safe transaction service where signatures are public. 3) Relayer executes T1: Safe.sol:168 nonce -> n+1, :170 checkSignatures, :175 G.checkTransaction sets active=true, :203 execute -> A. 4) A calls G.checkAfterExecution(bytes32(0), false) -> active=false (ReentrancyTransactionGuard.sol:67, no caller check). 5) A calls S.execTransaction(T2): signatures valid, G.checkTransaction sees active==false, T2 executes nested inside T1. DoS: attacker EOA calls G.checkTransaction(0,0,"",0,0,0,0,0,0,"",0) -> active=true; all Safes with guard G revert on execTransaction until G.checkAfterExecution is called by anyone; attacker re-locks after each unlock.
findings.evidence: ReentrancyTransactionGuard.sol:57-59 `GuardValue storage guard = getGuard(); require(!guard.active, "Reentrancy detected"); guard.active = true;` and :66-68 `function checkAfterExecution(bytes32, bool) external override { getGuard().active = false; }` — no msg.sender validation anywhere in the contract; GUARD_STORAGE_SLOT at :12 is a single constant slot. Safe.sol:168 (`nonce++` before execution), :175-190 (pre-check), :203 (execute), :226-228 (post-check). PoC: docs/security-review/poc/guards-reentrancy-debug.spec.ts, 'ReentrancyTransactionGuard' tests 1 and 2 (control run without the unlock call reverts with "Reentrancy detected"; with the unlock call the nested tx executes: mock.invocationCount()==1, safe.nonce()==n+2).
findings.recommendation: Key the flag by the calling Safe and only let the Safe that set it clear it: e.g. `mapping(address => bool) active;` with `require(!active[msg.sender]); active[msg.sender] = true;` in checkTransaction/checkModuleTransaction and `active[msg.sender] = false;` in the after-hooks (so an arbitrary caller can only toggle its own entry, which no Safe reads). Alternatively, store the flag in the Safe's own storage via a delegatecall-based design, or document prominently that this example is not safe to deploy as-is.

findings.title: ReentrancyTransactionGuard flag is global per guard deployment (not per Safe); a shared deployment blocks legitimate nested cross-Safe execution and NatSpec describes the slot incorrectly
findings.description: The in-flight flag lives at the constant slot keccak256("reentrancy_guard.guard.struct") in the guard contract's storage (:12, :29-37). It is not keyed by msg.sender (the Safe) and the same slot is used by both the transaction-guard path (:57-59) and the module-guard path (:87-89). The NatSpec at :26 claims the value "is stored in a slot that is unique to the contract instance and the function in which it is called", which is wrong on the second point (both functions share one slot) and misleading on the first (there is nothing per-Safe). Nothing in the contract, tests, or docs says one instance must be deployed per Safe; the contract has no constructor and looks like a singleton. If two Safes share one instance, a perfectly legitimate flow where Safe A executes a transaction whose target is Safe B's execTransaction (common when A is an owner/operator of B) reverts with "Reentrancy detected" because A's pre-check set the global flag. This also means the griefing in finding 1 affects every Safe sharing the deployment at once. Reproduced by PoC test "a shared guard deployment blocks legitimate nested Safe-calls-Safe execution".
findings.attack_path: Operational, not attacker-driven: Safe A and Safe B both set the same ReentrancyTransactionGuard instance. Owners sign T_B for B (nonce nB) and T_A for A (nonce nA, to = B, data = B.execTransaction(T_B, sigs)). Executing T_A: Safe.sol:175 -> G.checkTransaction sets active=true; execute -> B.execTransaction -> Safe.sol:175 -> G.checkTransaction -> require(!active) fails -> whole T_A reverts. Combined with finding 1, one attacker lock call halts all Safes on the shared instance simultaneously.
findings.evidence: ReentrancyTransactionGuard.sol:12 `bytes32 internal constant GUARD_STORAGE_SLOT = keccak256("reentrancy_guard.guard.struct");`, :26 NatSpec claim, :57-59 and :87-89 both operate on getGuard() with the same slot. PoC: docs/security-review/poc/guards-reentrancy-debug.spec.ts test 3 reverts with "Reentrancy detected" for distinct Safes A and B.
findings.recommendation: Key the flag by msg.sender (the Safe) as in finding 1, which makes a single deployment safe to share and keeps nested distinct-Safe flows working. Fix the NatSpec at :26 to describe the actual layout. If per-Safe deployment is the intended model, state that in the contract header and in docs/overview.md.

findings.title: DebugTransactionGuard.checkAfterExecution is permissionless and consumes the per-tx nonce record, so any callee can force the enclosing Safe transaction to revert
findings.description: checkTransaction stores `txNonces[txHash] = nonce` (:76) and checkAfterExecution (:84-89) does `require(nonce != 0, "Could not get nonce"); txNonces[txHash] = 0;` with no msg.sender check. The Safe tx hash is public/recomputable: the callee of a Safe transaction knows to=itself, value=msg.value, data=msg.data, operation=CALL, sees the gas params in the pending tx (zero in the common no-refund case) and can call ISafe(msg.sender).getTransactionHash(..., nonce()-1). It then calls guard.checkAfterExecution(txHash, false) directly, zeroing the record; when Safe.sol:227 calls checkAfterExecution for real, the require at :86 fails and the entire execTransaction reverts. Normally a Safe tx with safeTxGas>0 or gasPrice>0 tolerates a failing/malicious callee (Safe.sol:203-223 records ExecutionFailure and still pays the refund, burning the nonce); with this guard installed, any callee gains the ability to abort the outer transaction, unpay the relayer, and keep the nonce unburned, i.e. it converts the Safe's fail-safe semantics into a callee-controlled revert. The contract is labelled "only meant as a development tool and example" (:10), hence low. Reproduced by PoC test "a callee can force the whole Safe transaction to revert via permissionless checkAfterExecution".
findings.attack_path: 1) Safe S has DebugTransactionGuard G. 2) Owners sign T (to = contract C controlled by a third party, e.g. a token with hooks, a DEX, any integration). 3) execTransaction(T): Safe.sol:175 G.checkTransaction -> txNonces[H]=n (DebugTransactionGuard.sol:76). 4) execute -> C computes H via ISafe(msg.sender).getTransactionHash(address(this), msg.value, msg.data, 0, <gas params>, ISafe(msg.sender).nonce()-1) and calls G.checkAfterExecution(H,false) -> txNonces[H]=0. 5) Safe.sol:227 G.checkAfterExecution(H, success) -> require(0 != 0) fails -> whole Safe tx reverts regardless of safeTxGas/gasPrice settings.
findings.evidence: DebugTransactionGuard.sol:84-89: `function checkAfterExecution(bytes32 txHash, bool success) external override { uint256 nonce = txNonces[txHash]; require(nonce != 0, "Could not get nonce"); txNonces[txHash] = 0; emit GasUsage(...); }` — no caller check. PoC: docs/security-review/poc/guards-reentrancy-debug.spec.ts, DebugTransactionGuard test 1 reverts with "Could not get nonce".
findings.recommendation: Key txNonces by the Safe (`mapping(address => mapping(bytes32 => uint256))` indexed by msg.sender) so only the Safe that recorded the hash can consume it, or drop the require and the storage round-trip entirely (emit the nonce in the post event by recomputing it from msg.sender.nonce()), since a debug guard should never be able to revert the Safe.

findings.title: DebugTransactionGuard uses nonce 0 as its 'not recorded' sentinel, so a Safe transaction at nonce 0 always reverts when the guard is installed without consuming a nonce
findings.description: checkTransaction computes `nonce = safe.nonce() - 1` (:72; the Safe already incremented at Safe.sol:168) and stores it (:76). checkAfterExecution treats 0 as 'missing' (:86). For the Safe's first transaction nonce==0, so the record is 0 and the post-check reverts with "Could not get nonce". In the usual flow this is unreachable because installing the guard via execTransaction consumes nonce 0 and the cached `guard` at Safe.sol:172 (read before execution) means the installing tx itself is not checked; but the guard can be installed without consuming a nonce via a module (execTransactionFromModule -> Safe.setGuard, msg.sender==Safe passes `authorized`) or via a setup-time delegatecall library, after which the Safe's first execTransaction is bricked until the guard is removed through the same non-nonce path. Self-inflicted and limited to a development tool, hence informational; reproduced by PoC test "nonce 0 collides with the 'not set' sentinel".
findings.attack_path: Not attacker-driven. Owner deploys Safe with setup `to`/`data` enabling module M (nonce stays 0); M calls safe.execTransactionFromModule(safe, 0, setGuard(DebugGuard), CALL); first execTransaction at nonce 0 -> DebugTransactionGuard.sol:72 nonce = 1-1 = 0 -> txNonces[H]=0 -> Safe.sol:227 checkAfterExecution -> require(0 != 0) -> revert.
findings.evidence: DebugTransactionGuard.sol:72 `nonce = safe.nonce() - 1;`, :76 `txNonces[txHash] = nonce;`, :86 `require(nonce != 0, "Could not get nonce");`. PoC: docs/security-review/poc/guards-reentrancy-debug.spec.ts, DebugTransactionGuard test 2.
findings.recommendation: Store nonce+1 (or a separate 'seen' flag) so 0 is never a valid recorded value, or remove the record/require as suggested in finding 3.

result.ruled_out: 1) ReentrancyTransactionGuard flag stuck after a revert or after a failed inner call: if execTransaction reverts anywhere (guard pre-check, GS010, GS011/GS012 in handlePayment, the safeTxGas==0&&gasPrice==0 bubble at Safe.sol:207-216, or an OOG in the post-check) the whole tx reverts, so the guard's sstore is rolled back; if the inner execute merely returns false, Safe.sol continues to :227 and checkAfterExecution clears the flag. Module path identical (ModuleManager.sol:173-175, :187-204). No stuck-lock path from legitimate flows. 2) Guard removed or replaced mid-transaction: Safe.sol:172 caches `guard` before execute and :226 uses the cached value, so a tx that calls setGuard(0)/setGuard(new) still gets the old guard's checkAfterExecution (covered by test/core/Safe.GuardManager.spec.ts 'is called when removed'); ModuleManager.sol:173/175 and :187/204 cache `guard` and `guardHash` the same way. 3) Guard with no code silently passing: not possible — setGuard's supportsInterface call (GuardManager.sol:78) reverts for an EOA (0.7.6 extcodesize check; 0.8.x returndata-size check), and if a configured guard later loses its code (same-tx selfdestruct, EIP-7702 re-delegation) Safe.sol:175 reverts (verified with hardhat_setCode), bricking execTransaction including the setGuard(0) recovery path unless a module exists. This is the documented 'broken guard = DoS, design recovery mechanisms' risk (IGuardManager.sol:20-22, docs/overview.md:50-51), so not reported. 4) Guard checked after signatures/nonce: nonce++ at Safe.sol:168 precedes the guard call, but a guard revert reverts the whole tx so no nonce is burned; checkSignatures (:170) can only reach contract signers through staticcall (SecuredSignatureValidator), so a signer cannot swap the guard before it is read at :172. 5) Attacker-controllable inputs to checkTransaction: `msgSender` is the executor (any relayer) and `signatures` may carry trailing bytes beyond the `threshold*65` verified prefix (Safe.sol:319 only checks >=). No in-scope guard trusts either without verification: OnlyOwnersGuard verifies msgSender via Safe.isOwner; DebugTransactionGuard only emits signatures. Noted as a pitfall for third-party guards, not a defect. 6) OnlyOwnersGuard fooled by fallback handler or module: the guard's msg.sender is the Safe itself (Safe.sol:175 is a direct external call), and isOwner is implemented in OwnerManager on the Safe, not routed to the fallback handler; modules call execTransactionFromModule which never invokes the transaction guard (only the module guard, and OnlyOwnersGuard does not implement IModuleGuard so setModuleGuard rejects it with GS301). A nested self-call (Safe -> Safe.execTransaction) yields msgSender==Safe, and the Safe cannot be its own owner (OwnerManager GS203), so it is correctly rejected. 7) DelegateCallTransactionGuard bypass via MultiSend: if ALLOWED_TARGET is MultiSend (not MultiSendCallOnly), the inner batch may contain operation==1 entries that delegatecall arbitrary targets (MultiSend.sol:66-68), bypassing the restriction. This is the explicit trust model ('Limits delegate calls to a specific target' — the allowed target is trusted) and the reason MultiSendCallOnly exists (its header :6-7 says so); a configuration pitfall, not a code defect. Module-originated delegatecalls bypass the transaction guard by design (modules are trusted; the same contract can be installed as the module guard, ModuleManager.sol:120, where checkModuleTransaction applies the same rule at DelegateCallTransactionGuard.sol:68). Removing the guard via a CALL to self (setGuard(0)) is allowed and intended (test 'should revert on delegate call via Safe'). 8) Module guard ordering/hash plumbing: preModuleExecution returns (guard, guardHash) before execute; postModuleExecution passes exactly those to checkAfterModuleExecution; GS104 module check at :117 runs before the guard call so unauthorized callers never reach the guard; the onBeforeExecTransactionFromModule hook (SafeL2.sol:94 emits an event) runs before GS104 but a revert discards the event. result.ruled_out:
1. getTransactionHash 0x1901 trick (Safe.sol:539-546): struct hash is computed by keccak256(ptr,352) BEFORE being stored at ptr+64; mstore(ptr,0x1901) places 0x19 at ptr+30 and 0x01 at ptr+31; mstore(ptr+32,domainHash); keccak256(ptr+30,66) covers exactly [0x19,0x01]||domainHash||structHash. Correct. Dirty bits: to/gasToken/refundReceiver/operation are ABI-decoded calldata params (coder v1 cleans addresses and range-validates enums on load, also when getTransactionHash is reached internally from execTransaction with execTransaction's own decoded params); _nonce is uint256. data.offset/data.length are validated by the v1 calldata decoder (data_pointer+length<=calldatasize) and calldatacopy zero-pads anyway. Memory beyond FMP used temporarily, FMP untouched -> memory-safe honoured.
2. secp256r1 branch (Safe.sol:367-396): GS021/GS027 checks guarantee s+128<=signatures.length so the four mloads and keccak256(sig+0x40,0x40) stay in bounds; r/s are per-iteration locals re-assigned by signatureSplit each loop, so overwriting them in place is harmless. signerAddress receives a full 256-bit keccak, but Solidity cleans both operands of comparison operators (legacy cleanupNeededForOp / IR expressionAsType(forceCleanup)) so `currentOwner != signerAddress` compares the low 160 bits as intended; confirmed empirically by the passing [@secp256r1] tests (a non-cleaned compare would make every secp256r1 signature fail with GS028). qx/qy are validated on-curve by the precompile; address derivation from keccak(qx||qy) cannot be forged without a preimage.
3. EIP7951.p256Verify (EIP7951.sol:26-45): 160-byte input written beyond FMP temporarily; output to scratch 0x00..0x20; result := and(success, and(eq(returndatasize,0x20), eq(mload(0),1))) so an absent precompile (returndatasize 0) or a failed staticcall yields false, never a stale-memory true. result is 0/1 -> clean bool. No Solidity code depends on scratch persisting.
4. EIP7702.isThisDelegatedAccount (EIP7702.sol:23-26): extcodecopy(address(),0,0,3) writes only scratch bytes 0..2; shr(232, mload(0)) discards the 29 stale lower bytes; <3-byte code is zero-padded. Behaviour matches EIP-7702 EXTCODECOPY semantics (designator 0xef0100||addr). Used only in OwnerManager.requireIsValidOwner.
5. ErrorMessage.revertWithError (ErrorMessage.sol:23-30): Error(string) layout selector@+0, offset 0x20@+4, len 5@+0x24, bytes5 (left-aligned)@+0x44, revert size 0x64 = 4+32+32+32. All call sites pass string literals -> clean low bytes; even dirty padding would be ignored by decoders.
6. SecuredTokenTransfer.transferToken (SecuredTokenTransfer.sol:27-37): output region is scratch 0x00..0x20; returndatasize 0 -> success flag; 0x20 -> success && mload(0)!=0; otherwise false. Failed calls with 32-byte revert data are rejected via iszero(success). sub(gas(),10000) underflow is capped by EIP-150 (no revert). Any non-zero word (e.g. 2 or a dirty bool) is accepted as success -- lenient but gasToken is chosen/signed by owners and this is long-standing documented behaviour; no attack path, informational only, not reported.
7. SafeProxy.fallback (SafeProxy.sol:49-77): masterCopy branch writes shl(96,_singleton) at 0x6c so 0x60..0x6c (never-written zero slot) + 20 address bytes form a clean 32-byte ABI word; dirty high bits in slot 0 are discarded by the shl. Block is intentionally not memory-safe, overwrites 0x00.. including FMP, but always halts. Under 0.8/viaIR the missing annotation simply disables stack-to-memory for that function.
8. FallbackManager.fallback (FallbackManager.sol:58-85): calldatacopy(ptr,0,calldatasize) then mstore(ptr+calldatasize, shl(96,caller())) appends exactly 20 bytes (12 zero bytes follow but call length is calldatasize+20); returndatacopy uses returndatasize(); everything beyond FMP and the block halts. Non-payable fallback (callvalue check) is per IFallbackManager docs. The 1-3 byte calldata + appended sender selector-forging vector is the documented GS400 rationale (handler != self); for third-party handlers it is the documented trust assumption.
9. HandlerContext._msgSender (HandlerContext.sol:52-54): require(msg.data.length>=20); shr(96, calldataload(calldatasize-20)) yields a clean 20-byte address (calldataload zero-pads past calldatasize).
10. ModuleManager.execTransactionFromModuleReturnData (ModuleManager.sol:191-202): FMP bumped by returndatasize+0x20 before writing length and data; returndatacopy size == returndatasize; nothing between execute() and the copy touches returndata. Non-word-aligned FMP is permitted. Return-bomb from the module's chosen target only hurts the (trusted) module's own call. getModulesPaginated mstore(array,moduleCount) shrinks a Solidity-allocated array; moduleCount>=1 whenever next!=SENTINEL, so array[moduleCount-1] cannot underflow.
11. StorageAccessible (StorageAccessible.sol:23-26, 38-46): getStorageAt writes inside the allocated result; a length>=2^251 makes `length<<5` wrap so the loop would write past the small allocation, but memory expansion OOGs long before any effect and the function is view -> no impact. simulateAndRevert delegatecalls arbitrary code in Safe context but unconditionally reverts (post-Cancun SELFDESTRUCT also reverted); ptr region used after the call, then halts.
12. CompatibilityFallbackHandler.simulate (CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:118-177) incl. #1123: calldatasize>=4 guaranteed by dispatch so sub(calldatasize,4) cannot underflow; output region [0x00,0x40) is exactly scratch; `or(success, lt(returndatasize,0x40))` guards non-Safe callers; responseEncodedSize=mload(0x20)+0x20 and returndatacopy(response,0x20,size) matches a Safe's [success][len][data] layout and an oversized len simply makes returndatacopy fault (documented); response allocated by bumping FMP; revert(add(response,0x20), mload(response)) now returns exactly len bytes (the pre-#1123 extra 32 bytes were only trailing garbage, ignored by Error(string) decoders). Add overflow of mload(0x20)+0x20 only reachable for non-Safe callers (documented undefined behaviour). Verified by the passing "should propagate exact revert data" test.
13. MarshalLib.decodeWithSelector (MarshalLib.sol:60): selector := shl(168, shr(160,data)) leaves original bits 160..215 inside the bytes4 variable's low bits (dirty) if a caller stores a non-canonical bytes32. Only consumer is ERC165Handler.addSupportedInterfaceBatch (ERC165Handler.sol:60-65): selector is used as a mapping key (compiler cleans), in an event (cleans), XORed into interfaceId and then compared with == (cleans), and inputs come from the Safe itself under onlySelf -> benign. decode() masks handler with 160-bit mask and isStatic is 0/1. SignatureVerifierMuxer sigSelector (L102) is a dirty bytes4 from calldataload but is only used in an == comparison (cleaned).
14. MultiSend/MultiSendCallOnly loop (MultiSend.sol:38-77): operation/to extracted with shr (clean); loop condition lt(i,length) compares an offset that includes the 0x20 length word, so up to 32 trailing bytes are silently ignored and 33..84 trailing bytes would be parsed as a garbage entry reading beyond the array; the whole payload is owner-signed and this is identical to the audited 1.3.0/1.4.1 code -> malformed-input behaviour, not an attack. Unknown operation leaves success=0 and reverts with stale returndata (harmless). to==0 -> address(this) default is the documented self-call feature.
15. SignatureDecoder.signatureSplit (SignatureDecoder.sol:25-30): caller checks signatures.length>=requiredSignatures*65 (SafeMath) and i<requiredSignatures, so r/s/v reads are in bounds; byte(0,...) yields a clean uint8; the extra 31 bytes read past the array are discarded.
16. checkContractSignature (Safe.sol:270-296): GS022 ensures offset+32<=len before reading the inner length, GS023 ensures offset+32+innerLen<=len; contractSignature is a view pointer into signatures and abi.encodeWithSelector copies innerLen bytes -> in bounds. SecuredSignatureValidator (#1115): `success && result.length == 32 && abi.decode(...) == bytes32(magic)` short-circuits so abi.decode never sees <32 bytes; staticcall semantics unchanged (function was already view -> STATICCALL); EOA/precompile/reverting/return-bombing targets all map to GS024 and cannot produce a false positive (checked identity, sha256, ripemd160, modexp, ecrecover, bn/BLS, blake2f, KZG, p256verify output shapes vs the magic word; abi.encodeWithSelector pads to 100+32k bytes so fixed-size precompile inputs never match). The stricter 32-byte/clean-magic requirement is a documented breaking change (CHANGELOG.md L15) with no new consequence beyond the documented compatibility note. Self-signature recursion for 7702 self-owned Safes is gas-bounded and needs a real signature at the base, covered by existing tests.
17. Executor.execute, CreateCall, SafeProxyFactory.deployProxy, SafeToL2Setup, SafeMigration, guard sload/sstore, ReentrancyTransactionGuard.getGuard, SimulateTxAccessor.simulate: trivial, bounds come from Solidity-managed bytes (add(data,0x20)/mload(data)), returndatacopy sizes equal returndatasize(), sstore values are ABI-decoded (clean) addresses, FMP updated where memory is retained.
18. execTransaction gas arithmetic (Safe.sol:197,203): GS010 guarantees >=3000 gas before `gasleft()-2500` so no underflow in 0.7 and no panic in 0.8; `(safeTxGas<<6)/63` and `safeTxGas+2500` can only wrap for owner-signed absurd values (>=2^250) where the 63/64 cap already bounds the callee gas -- no attack path.
19. Solidity 0.8.x/viaIR: every block except SafeProxy is annotated memory-safe and only touches scratch (0x00-0x3f), Solidity-allocated arrays, or memory at/after the FMP (bumping it when retained), so stack-to-memory relocation is safe; SafeProxy halts inside its block. Shift operators are unchecked in 0.8 too, so no new panics in the assembly-adjacent arithmetic beyond the owner-signed absurd values noted in 18.

findings.title: docs/signatures.md does not document the v == 2 (secp256r1 / EIP-7951) signature type added in 1.5.0
findings.description: docs/signatures.md is the canonical description of the packed signature format ("Each signature has a constant length of 65 bytes ..."). It lists ECDSA (`31 > signature type > 26`, line 15), eth_sign (`> 30`, line 27), contract signatures (`== 0`, line 39) and pre-validated (`== 1`, line 61). Safe 1.5.0 added a fifth branch in contracts/Safe.sol:354-396: `v == 2` means `r` is the owner address and `s` is a data pointer to a fixed 128-byte dynamic part `{r}{s}{qx}{qy}` with NO length prefix (unlike contract signatures, which have one). This type is absent from the document (only docs/error_codes.md:50-55 mentions secp256r1 at all). Off-chain tooling, indexers, guards or relayers that parse Safe signature blobs per the documentation will mis-decode a 1.5.0 blob containing a `v = 2` entry (treating `r`/`s` as a secp256k1 signature, or mis-computing where the dynamic part begins) and may, for example, mis-attribute signers in UIs/simulations.
findings.attack_path: No on-chain attack path; the contract code is authoritative and strict (GS021/GS027/GS028). Risk is limited to third-party parsers written from the documentation producing wrong signer attribution for secp256r1-signed transactions.
findings.evidence: docs/signatures.md:13-69 enumerates only types 0, 1, 27-30 and >30. contracts/Safe.sol:354-368: `} else if (v == 2) { ... currentOwner = address(uint160(uint256(r))); ... if (uint256(s) < requiredSignatures.mul(65)) revertWithError("GS021"); if (uint256(s).add(128) > signatures.length) revertWithError("GS027");` and lines 381-393 read `r, s, qx, qy` from `signatures + s + 0x20` with no length word.
findings.recommendation: Add a `secp256r1 Signature (signature type == 2)` section to docs/signatures.md describing the constant part `{32-bytes owner address}{32-bytes data position}{0x02}` and the fixed 128-byte dynamic part `{r}{s}{qx}{qy}` (no length prefix), and that the owner address must equal the last 20 bytes of `keccak256(qx || qy)`.

findings.title: SignMessageLib NatSpec describes a verification path (pre-image + empty signature) that no longer exists; only abi.encode(bytes32)-shaped messages are verifiable via ERC-1271
findings.description: SignMessageLib.sol:27 states the on-chain signed message "Can be verified using EIP-1271 validation method by passing the pre-image of the message hash and empty bytes as the signature". Since 1.4.0 (CHANGELOG.md:107-111) the legacy `isValidSignature(bytes,bytes)` was removed; the only ERC-1271 entry point is `CompatibilityFallbackHandler.isValidSignature(bytes32 _dataHash, bytes _signature)` (CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:73-86), which hashes `encodeMessageDataForSafe(safe, abi.encode(_dataHash))` (line 76). Therefore `signMessage(_data)` (SignMessageLib.sol:30-34, hash = SafeMessage{message:_data}) is only verifiable on-chain if `_data` is exactly the 32-byte `_dataHash`; an arbitrary pre-image signed per the NatSpec can never be verified (`Hash not approved`). Confirmed by PoC docs/security-review/poc/replay-lens.spec.ts ("SignMessageLib: only abi.encode(hash)-shaped messages are verifiable"). This fails closed and has no exploit path, but misleads integrators and the ExtensibleFallbackHandler default path (SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:147-153) has the same 32-byte wrapping.
findings.attack_path: None (fails closed). An integrator following the NatSpec would mark a non-32-byte pre-image as signed and later find ERC-1271 verification impossible, a liveness/UX issue only.
findings.evidence: SignMessageLib.sol:27 `@dev Can be verified using EIP-1271 validation method by passing the pre-image of the message hash and empty bytes as the signature.` vs CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:76 `bytes memory messageData = encodeMessageDataForSafe(safe, abi.encode(_dataHash));` and :78-79 `if (_signature.length == 0) { require(safe.signedMessages(messageHash) != 0, "Hash not approved"); }`.
findings.recommendation: Update the NatSpec to say the message must be the ABI-encoded 32-byte hash that will later be passed to `isValidSignature(bytes32,bytes)` (i.e. `signMessage(abi.encode(hash))`), and cross-reference `CompatibilityFallbackHandler.getMessageHash`.
